takeaway: InvisiFlow routes low-priority telemetry toward less-congested neighboring buffers, exploiting spare paths to reduce monitoring-data loss while leaving user traffic prioritized.
background: Fine-grained network monitoring sends switch-generated telemetry to a small set of collectors over the same fabric as user traffic. The transmission channel must preserve useful records without congesting applications.
villain: Shortest-path telemetry either competes at normal priority and delays user flows or runs at low priority and is starved or dropped on busy links.
approach: Each switch stores telemetry in a programmable egress-register buffer and periodically sends lowest-priority pull requests containing its buffer use to every neighbor. A neighbor with more buffered telemetry replies with data, so records move down local congestion gradients; collectors advertise zero occupancy, and a distance-based slope discourages oscillation. Shared egress storage lets a payload be attached only when a low-priority packet can be scheduled on a port in that pipeline, while optional spare servers can absorb excess data.
impact: The authors argue that this content- and topology-agnostic channel can improve monitoring accuracy by harvesting network-wide spare capacity without changing user-traffic forwarding.

evaluation.overview: The authors evaluate telemetry loss, monitoring accuracy, delay, user-flow completion time, and robustness in ns-3 simulations and a programmable-switch testbed.
evaluation.implemented: A roughly 600-line P4-16 switch program on two Wedge100BF-32X switches, with DPDK collectors and optional storage servers.
evaluation.setting: Simulations use a 144-server, 100-Gbps FatTree with 4:1 oversubscription under Hadoop and ML workloads; the hardware testbed virtualizes four leaves and two spines over 10-Gbps links.
baselines: Low-priority UDP with OrbWeaver packet generation and packet spraying
Pull-based shortest-path transmission without congestion gradients

results.text: The authors report that, at 70% load in the default FatTree setting, InvisiFlow's missing-path ratio was 33.8× lower than low-priority UDP and 36.3× lower than pull-based shortest-path transmission.

The authors report that, with the testbed's shortest collector path fully occupied by user traffic, InvisiFlow had 0% telemetry loss versus more than 97% for low-priority UDP, while both added less than 0.1% user-flow completion-time overhead.

limitations: Because telemetry remains lowest priority, delivery and latency are unbounded: if every port stays busy, packets can drop, and time-sensitive reports need restricted routing or a fallback channel. Each distinct collector group needs its own switch-buffer allocation, and the prototype's register design assumes small records under 160 B or per-hop segmentation.
phd_group_signal: This work exemplifies a networking-systems style that turns queueing theory into data-plane mechanisms, then tests application accuracy and traffic interference in simulation and hardware.

claims.text: InvisiFlow exchanges low-priority neighbor pull requests carrying telemetry-buffer occupancy; a higher-occupancy neighbor returns telemetry, while shared egress-register storage lets a payload be attached when a low-priority packet is scheduled on a port in that pipeline.

The design targets telemetry that tolerates asynchronous, out-of-order, and potentially arbitrarily delayed delivery; it cannot guarantee delivery when no spare bandwidth exists, and separate collector groups consume separate buffer allocations.
claims.locator: PDF p. 5 and p. 13 (paper pp. 74 and 82); §3.1 and §7

claims.text: The P4 prototype stores telemetry in egress register arrays and assumes records smaller than 160 B; the paper proposes per-hop segmentation for larger messages.
